verses.note: The story of humanity outside the garden begins here. Genesis will keep moving people east, away from God's presence (4:16, 11:2), and Israel's own later exile from its land repeats this first banishment.

Cain goes out "from the presence of the LORD", further east than his parents. Genesis keeps tracking eastward movement away from God (11:2), and the reversal of that exile is one of Scripture's great hopes.
The family is saved by going down into a foreign land. The pattern of a remnant preserved outside the land, and brought through it, returns in Israel's later history in Babylon.
The brothers name themselves as sojourners, not settlers. Israel's law later bases its care for foreigners on this memory, since Israel had been a ger in Egypt (Exodus 22:21, Deuteronomy 10:19).

The return to Egypt is a reminder that the promise is not yet fulfilled. The family has a grave in Canaan and a home in Egypt, and God's word of 15:13-14 still stands: they will be strangers in a land not their own until God brings them out.

Exile is God's judgment carried out through Babylon's armies. The verse names both causes the prophets gave for it, violence (blood) and idolatry, and insists that God, not Nebuchadnezzar, is the one who scattered.

Exile is not God's last word. The gathering of Israel from the nations is promised in the law itself (Deuteronomy 30:3-5) and throughout the prophets, and the return under Cyrus after 539 BC was its first installment.
